title: Yesterday, and the past tense
goal: Talking about what has already happened — with a past tense that, unlike the present, marks who did it at the END of the verb.
bekal: building past-tense verbs for all eight persons
using كان to put sentences with no verb into the past
telling the story of a whole day, start to finish

dialogs.title: حوار — بعد العزومة
dialogs.intro: Saturday morning, the day after Budi was invited to dinner at Mona's family home. Ahmad asks how it went.

lines.speaker: أحمد:
lines.id: What did you do yesterday? Where did you go?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: رحت بيت منى. عزمونا على العشا.
lines.id: I went to Mona's. They invited us to dinner.
lines.literal: I-went house Mona. they-invited-us to dinner.

lines.speaker: أحمد:
lines.id: Really? And what did you eat?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: ماما بتاعتها عملت ملوخية وفراخ ورز.
lines.baca: maama bitaa‘t-ha ‘amalit mulukheyya wi firaakh wi ruzz.
lines.id: Her mom made molokhia, chicken, and rice.
lines.literal: mom of-her she-made molokhia and chicken and rice.

lines.speaker: أحمد:
lines.text: وعجبتك الملوخية؟ كتير من الأجانب مابيحبوهاش.
lines.baca: wi ‘agabitak il-mulukheyya? kitiir min il-agaanib mabyihibbuhaash.
lines.id: And did you like the molokhia? A lot of foreigners don't.
lines.literal: and it-pleased-you the-molokhia? many of the-foreigners not-they-like-it.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: في الأول اتخضيت من اللون! بس دقتها وحبيتها.
lines.baca: fil-awwil itkhaḍēt mil-lōn! bas du’t-ha wi habbēt-ha.
lines.id: At first the color gave me a fright! But I tasted it and loved it.
lines.literal: at the-first I-got-startled from the-color! but I-tasted-it and I-loved-it.

lines.speaker: أحمد:
lines.id: Haha. And how late did you stay?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: لحد بعد نص الليل. شربنا شاي وحكينا كتير.
lines.baca: lihadd ba‘d nuṣṣ il-lēl. shiribna shaay wi hakēna kitiir.
lines.id: Until after midnight. We drank tea and talked a lot.
lines.literal: until after half the-night. we-drank tea and we-talked a-lot.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: أيوه. كان بيسألني عن إندونيسيا طول الوقت.
lines.baca: aywa. kaan biyis’alni ‘an Indunisya ṭuul il-wa’t.
lines.id: Yes. He kept asking me about Indonesia the whole time.
lines.literal: yes. he-was he-asks-me about Indonesia length the-time.

lines.speaker: أحمد:
lines.text: طبعاً. المصريين بيحبوا يسألوا. ورجعت إزاي؟
lines.baca: ṭab‘an. il-maṣriyyiin biyhibbu yis’alu. wi rigi‘t izzaay?
lines.id: Of course. Egyptians love asking questions. And how did you get home?
lines.literal: of-course. the-Egyptians they-like they-ask. and you-returned how?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: أخوها وصلني بالعربية. ماخدش مني فلوس.
lines.baca: akhuuha waṣṣalni bil-‘arabeyya. makhadsh minni fuluus.
lines.id: Her brother drove me. He wouldn't take any money from me.
lines.literal: brother-her he-delivered-me by-the-car. not-he-took from-me money.

lines.speaker: أحمد:
lines.text: أكيد ماخدش! انت ضيف. ده عيب عندنا.
lines.id: Of course he wouldn't! You're a guest. That's not done here.
lines.literal: sure not-he-took! you guest. this shame with-us.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: Honestly, I felt a bit awkward.

lines.speaker: أحمد:
lines.id: Don't feel awkward. Next time, you invite them.

notes: **The past tense marks the doer at the END, not the front.** Compare بشرب (I drink) with شربت (I drank). The prefix disappears and a suffix shows up. It's the exact mirror of the present tense, and once you see the pattern, the whole system falls into place.

**The word كان puts a sentence with no verb into the past.** أنا طالب (I'm a student) becomes كنت طالب (I was a student). It also goes in front of a بـ-verb for past habits: كان بيسألني (he kept asking me).

**The word عزم means to invite, and عزومة is the dinner invitation itself.** It's one of the key words of Egyptian social life. Being invited to someone's home is a sign of real friendship, and turning it down without a good reason is rare.

**The word عيب means socially "not done", not religiously "forbidden".** It governs thousands of small things in Egyptian manners: taking money from a guest is عيب, letting a guest carry their own plate is عيب. The opposite: ماشي or عادي.

**The word اتكسف means embarrassed in the sense of shy or awkward, not ashamed of doing wrong.** For that, people use اتحرج or خجلان. The negative command ماتتكسفش is the line Egyptian hosts say to guests more than any other.
**The word بصراحة means "honestly, frankly", and it's almost a filler.** Egyptians use it to open a personal opinion, sometimes several times in one paragraph. Its cousin: الحقيقة *il-ha’ii’a*.

grammars.title: The past tense, eight persons
body: The endings are the same for every verb. Only the verb's body differs, and you've been memorizing those in pairs since unit seven.
after: Notice that أنا and انت use exactly the same ending: كتبت means both "I wrote" and "you wrote". The pronoun is usually said only when there's a chance of confusion; otherwise context does the job.
The هي form is spelled the same way too — كتبت — but it's said differently: *katabt* for I and you, *katabit* for she. Once again, your ear tells them apart, not your eye.
To make it negative, use the same wrap as in the present: ماكتبتش (I didn't write), ماشربش (he didn't drink), ماعملناش (we didn't do).

grammars.title: The verb كان — and five things it can do
body: The verb كان is the only way to move a sentence with no verb into the past, and it also powers a few other patterns.
after: The form of كان for I is **كنت** *kunt*, for we **كنا** *kunna*, for they **كانوا** *kaanu*. It's one of the hollow verbs that shorten — the same pattern as راح becoming رحت and نام becoming نمت.
Row seven shows something unexpected: even فيه, which never changes, goes into the past by putting كان in front of it, and that كان stays masculine singular. The negative is ماكانش فيه.

blocks.text: The phrase اللي فات means "that passed", and it works with any unit of time. Notice that it agrees with its noun: الأسبوع اللي فات for the masculine week, and السنة اللي فاتت for the feminine year.

blocks.title: The word لسه works two ways
items: Followed by a past verb, لسه means "just": لسه وصلت (I just got here), لسه أكلت (I just ate).
Followed by an adjective or noun, لسه means "still": لسه صغير (still small), لسه في الجامعة (still at university).
Standing alone as an answer, لسه means "not yet": متجوز؟ — لسه.

blocks.text: These sentences are a storytelling frame you can refill with any verb. Notice that they're all in the past tense.

The last line is a typically warm Egyptian expression: نمت زي القتيل, "I slept like a murdered man", for a very deep sleep. Egyptian Arabic is full of over-the-top comparisons like this, and using them makes you sound instantly more alive.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right form of كان.

items: What did you do yesterday? (to a man)
We drank tea and talked a lot.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

عملت إيه إمبارح؟ — رحت بيت منى. — عزمونا على العشا. — شربنا شاي وحكينا كتير. — رجعت بعد نص الليل.
